first_impression.reaction: The first line is literally my search, and the answer straight after it is 'yes'. That's what I wanted. It's dated October 2026 and it names Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department, so I believe it. Honestly I could have closed the tab after one sentence. I stayed because the Key Takeaways raised something I didn't know about (the surname thing), so I read those, then skipped to the surname section, then had a quick look at the FAQ.

journey.quote: Is marriage in Italy recognised in Australia? In most cases, yes: an overseas marriage is generally recognised here if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law, according to both Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department.
journey.reaction: Answer in the first sentence, with the government named. No scrolling past fluff. Perfect.

journey.quote: This guide covers recognition, proof, surnames and later celebrations, as at October 2026.
journey.reaction: Is this still true in 2026? It tells me. And I know what's coming, so I can jump straight to the bit I care about.

journey.quote: An Italian marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid under Italian law and would have been valid here, the test set by Part VA of the Marriage Act 1961.
journey.reaction: Same answer as the intro, just with an Act name tacked on. Fine, but I'd already got it. The next three bullets are the useful ones.

journey.quote: You cannot register an Italian marriage in Australia, so bring home the comune's marriage certificate with a Prefettura apostille and have it translated in full.
journey.reaction: That's a to-do list I can actually use. Certificate, apostille, translation. I'd screenshot this.

journey.quote: If you were born in Australia and want your partner's surname on your passport, the Passport Office always needs a name change certificate from an Australian registry.
journey.reaction: Wait, really? I didn't know that. This is the line that made me keep reading. Now I want to know how long that takes and what it costs.

journey.section: Is an Italian marriage recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: Yes, in most cases, with no form to lodge when you land.
journey.reaction: Heading matches my question, and the first words answer it again. Good to know there's nothing to file.

journey.section: Do you need to register an Italian marriage in Australia?
journey.quote: Before you leave Italy, ask for the comune's certificate, not the parish's.
journey.reaction: Very practical. Exactly the sort of thing I'd get wrong.

journey.section: The legal test: what the Marriage Act says
journey.quote: Under s 88D(2), the marriage is not recognised if, at the time of the wedding:
journey.reaction: Section numbers on my phone. I skimmed the bullets, saw 'still married to someone else', thought 'not me', and moved on. Not a problem, just not for me.

journey.quote: Born here: an Australian registry name change certificate. Born overseas and a citizen before marrying: a legalised certificate, translated in full
journey.reaction: Useful, but that's a lot of text crammed into a table cell. On my phone the table goes sideways and I lose which row I'm in.

journey.section: Marriage certificate, atto or multilingual extract
journey.quote: Not published: whether any Australian agency accepts an Italian multilingual extract on its own.
journey.reaction: I don't know what a multilingual extract is and now I'm told nobody knows if it works. I'd have skipped this paragraph if I'd known.

journey.section: Changing your surname after marrying in Italy
journey.quote: The NSW registry says so directly: an overseas certificate cannot be used to change your surname, but "this does not mean that your marriage is not recognised in Australia".
journey.reaction: Good, that clears up the panic. The marriage is fine, the name is the separate bit.

journey.section: Changing your surname after marrying in Italy
journey.quote: In NSW you apply for an official change of name, as set out in the NSW registry's guidance on overseas marriages.
journey.reaction: Okay, but how much does it cost and how long does it take? Just tell me. Nothing on fees or timing anywhere in this section.

journey.section: Travel in the name on your passport
journey.quote: Book the honeymoon in your current names and sort out the name change once home.
journey.reaction: Love this. One line, solves an actual problem.

journey.quote: Not published: Prefettura processing times. Ask your Wedded Advisor to build the appointment into your plan.
journey.reaction: I don't know who the Wedded Advisor is. Feels like a little sales nudge dropped into a government-info section. Not a big deal once, though.

journey.quote: No. Smartraveller says marrying an Australian citizen does not ensure entry or citizenship; immigration law still applies.
journey.reaction: Short, direct, sourced. The FAQ is what I'd come back to.

unanswered_questions: How much does a change of name application cost, and how long does it take, in NSW or Victoria (roughly, as at 2026)?
What does an apostille from the Prefettura and a full NAATI translation of the certificate cost, even as a ballpark?
Does any of this change if only one of us is Australian, or if we both live overseas (e.g. in Singapore) rather than in Australia?
If I don't change my surname at all, do I need to do anything with the Italian certificate once home?

turn_offs_found.why: Long sentences squeezed into table cells. The two tables are hard to read on a phone on the train.

turn_offs_found.quote: In NSW you apply for an official change of name, as set out in the NSW registry's guidance on overseas marriages.
turn_offs_found.why: The surname section tells me I have to apply but not what it costs or how long it takes, which is the very next thing I want to know.

would_share_with: My partner, the Key Takeaways and the line about booking the honeymoon in current names
A friend who is getting married in Italy and asked me the same question

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, speak with a Wedded Advisor about which route suits you.
cta_reaction.why: I got my answer, so I'd bookmark the page, not talk to someone. The 'marry at home first or in Italy' choice is interesting and I might come back when we're actually deciding, but right now I don't know this brand and I'm not handing over my details for a question I've already had answered.

top_3_changes: In the surname section, say roughly what a change of name application costs and how long it takes (with an 'as at' date and source), or say plainly that it varies by state and link the fee page, because that is the very next question after 'you need to apply'.
Make the two tables phone-friendly: turn 'Which proof suits which purpose' into short bullets, or cut each cell down to a few words.
Add one line saying whether the answer changes if only one partner is Australian or the couple lives overseas, since the page assumes both of you live in Australia.
